draft.title: Gravimetric analysis
card: Gravimetric analysis finds how much of a substance is in a sample by measuring mass. The substance is turned into a solid precipitate that is pure and has a known formula.
The steps are: add excess reagent so all of the ion precipitates, filter the solid, wash it, dry it and weigh it. Drying until the mass stops changing shows that all the water has gone.
The mass of the precipitate is converted to moles using its molar mass. The mole ratio in the balanced equation then gives the moles of the ion in the sample.
For example, chloride ions can be precipitated as silver chloride, AgCl, by adding excess silver nitrate. One mole of AgCl contains one mole of chloride ions.
draft.remember: Precipitate all of the ion, dry and weigh it, then use moles to work back to the amount in the sample.

a.q: Why is the precipitate dried until its mass stops changing before the final weighing?
opts: So that no water is left to add extra mass
So that the precipitate fully dissolves again
So that more precipitate forms during drying
So that the molar mass of the precipitate drops
a.why: A wet precipitate would weigh more than the solid alone, so the amount of ion would seem too high. A steady mass shows the water has gone. Drying does not make more precipitate or change its molar mass.
a.clue: Think about what else could be adding mass to the solid.

b.q: A 50.0 mL water sample from a bore in Broken Hill is treated with excess silver nitrate. The dried AgCl precipitate has a mass of 0.287 g (molar mass 143.4 g/mol). How many moles of chloride ions were in the sample?
b.why: Moles of AgCl = 0.287 ÷ 143.4 = 0.00200 mol. The ratio of AgCl to Cl⁻ is 1 to 1, so the sample held 0.00200 mol of chloride. Halving the answer would wrongly treat the ratio as 2 to 1.
b.clue: Divide the mass by the molar mass, then check the mole ratio.

a.best: So that no water is left to add extra mass
